title: The Art of Probing and Summarizing
overview: Chapter 5 completes Egan's set of basic communication skills with probing and summarising. It opens by framing all helping as influence and, borrowing Thaler and Sunstein's idea of the nudge and libertarian paternalism, casts helpers as choice architects whose skills exert 'gentle power'. It then covers prompts (verbal and nonverbal), the four forms of probes (statements, requests, questions, single words), how to use questions well, and a series of guidelines for probing, from using feedback and building concreteness to filling in missing pieces, getting a balanced view, moving clients to useful stages and inviting self-challenge, before showing how probes must be mixed with empathy (Box 5.1). The second half explains summarising: when helpers should summarise and why clients should sometimes do it themselves, illustrated through Mara and Carlos. It closes with the shadow side of communication skills (necessary but not sufficient; relationship versus technology) and advice on developing real proficiency through everyday practice.
objectives: Explain nudging, libertarian paternalism and the helper as choice architect.
Define prompts and probes and distinguish verbal and nonverbal prompts.
Describe and illustrate the four forms of probes.
State Egan's guidelines for using questions, including open-ended and closed questions.
Explain the guidelines and goals for using probes, including Box 5.1.
Describe how empathic responses and probes should be combined in practice.
Explain when and how to use summaries, including client-provided summaries.
Analyse the Mara and Carlos excerpt as an illustration of probing and summarising.
Discuss the shadow side of communication skills and how proficiency is developed.

sections.heading: Nudging
sections.detailed:
Egan opens the chapter by recalling a point from Chapter 2: every attempt to help another person involves some degree of influence. Helpers inevitably influence their clients. The real question is how to influence them well, so that clients discuss difficult problems, develop new life-enhancing perspectives on themselves, others and the world, work on the right issues, explore possibilities for a better future, choose and commit to problem-managing goals, explore ways of reaching those goals and take effective action, all without being robbed of their freedom.

Libertarian paternalism. To describe this kind of influence Egan borrows from Thaler and Sunstein (2008) and their book Nudge. They call it libertarian paternalism. The influence side is in a sense paternalistic, and the freedom side is libertarian. Egan stresses two qualifications: paternalism here does not mean coercion, physical or psychological, and libertarian does not mean "do whatever you want".

Helpers as choice architects. Thaler and Sunstein speak of choice architects, people responsible for organising the context in which others make decisions. Because decision making is one of the key ingredients of successful therapy, Egan argues it is important to look at how helpers shape the context of clients' decisions. Since helpers cannot avoid influencing clients, they are choice architects whether they like it or not. Treatment models, including the Skilled Helper framework and the methods and communication skills that make it work, are different forms of choice architecture. In the hands of savvy, principled helpers, the model, methods and skills of any approach can serve as nudges.

What a nudge is. Thaler and Sunstein define a nudge as any feature of the choice architecture that changes behaviour in a predictable way without forbidding any options. Egan adds that the predictability meant is that of the social sciences, not the physical sciences.

Empathy as a nudge. Egan shows that an empathic response already works as a nudge in two ways. First, because a helper cannot respond empathically to everything a client says, choosing what to respond to is itself a form of influence (selective responding). Second, empathic responses tend to encourage clients to explore the issue more broadly or deeply. Yet empathic responses do not pin clients down.

Gentle power. Nudges have power, but it is gentle. Used skilfully, nudges promote collaboration rather than block it, do not overwhelm clients and keep the client at the centre of decision making. Egan announces that the two skills of this chapter, probing and summarising, are often used as nudges, and that their gentle power, rightly used, can greatly benefit clients.
sections.simple: All helping involves influencing clients. Egan, using Thaler and Sunstein's idea of a nudge, says helpers should influence clients gently and predictably without taking away their freedom or any of their options. Helpers are choice architects, and probes and summaries are two of their main nudges.
keyPoints: All helping involves influence; the aim is to influence without robbing clients of freedom.
Thaler and Sunstein (2008) call this libertarian paternalism: not coercion, and not 'do whatever you want'.
A choice architect organises the context in which people decide; helpers and treatment models are choice architecture.
A nudge alters behaviour predictably without forbidding any options.
Empathic responses nudge through selective responding and by prompting deeper exploration.
Nudges have 'gentle' power: they foster collaboration and keep clients at the centre of decisions.

sections.heading: The Art of Probing
sections.detailed:
In most of the examples Egan used for sharing empathic responses (Chapter 4), clients explored themselves fairly easily. That is not always the case. Helpers must respond with empathy when clients do reveal themselves, but at times they also need to nudge, encourage or prompt clients to explore their concerns when clients do not do so on their own. So the ability to use prompts and probes well is another important communication skill. Egan's image: if empathic responding is the lubricant of the dialogue, probes supply the nudges that are often needed.

Definition. Prompts and probes are verbal, and sometimes nonverbal, tactics that help clients talk more freely and concretely about any issue at any stage of the helping process. They are not limited to the opening stage of telling the story.

What probes can do across the process. Egan lists several uses: helping clients identify and explore opportunities they have been overlooking, clearing up blind spots, translating dreams into realistic goals, developing realistic plans for accomplishing goals, and working through obstacles to action. Used judiciously, probes give focus and direction to the whole helping process.

Probing therefore links the skills of Chapters 3 and 4 (tuning in, listening, empathy) to the later stages of the Skilled Helper model (new perspectives, goals, strategies, action). The chapter moves from the lightest forms (prompts) to fuller probes (statements, requests, questions, single words), then to how to use questions, guidelines for probing, and the balance between probing and empathy.
sections.simple: Some clients do not open up on their own, so helpers need to prompt and probe. Prompts and probes are verbal or nonverbal moves that help clients talk more freely and concretely at any stage of helping. If empathy oils the conversation, probes give it a push.
keyPoints: Probing is needed when clients do not explore their concerns spontaneously.
Empathy is the 'lubricant' of dialogue; probes provide the needed nudges.
Prompts and probes are verbal and sometimes nonverbal tactics for freer, more concrete talk at any stage.
Probes help clients find overlooked opportunities, clear blind spots, turn dreams into goals, make plans and work through obstacles.
Used judiciously, probes give focus and direction to the whole helping process.

sections.heading: Verbal and Nonverbal Prompts
sections.detailed:
Egan defines prompts as brief verbal or nonverbal interventions meant to let clients know the helper is with them and to encourage them to keep talking. They are the lightest form of probing.

Nonverbal prompts. A counsellor's nonverbal behaviour can work like a probe. Egan's example: a client struggling to make a peace overture to a neighbour he or she is at odds with says, "I just can't do it!" The helper says nothing, simply leans forward attentively and waits. After a pause the client explains that taking the first step would feel like giving in, like weakness, and the two go on to explore how a well-handled overture could be a sign of strength instead. Body movements, gestures, nods, eye movements and similar behaviours can all serve as nonverbal prompts or nudges.

Vocal and verbal prompts. Sounds and words such as "um", "uh-huh", "sure", "yes", "I see", "ah", "okay" and "oh" can act as prompts, with one condition: they must be used intentionally, not as a sign that attention is drifting, that the helper does not know what else to do, or that he or she is on automatic pilot. In Egan's example a 33-year-old married woman struggling with perfectionism at work and at home doubts she can keep the contract she made with herself to let trivial things go. The helper says only a brief "Um" and stays silent. The client pauses, laughs at the irony of a perfectionist saying she "can't" do something, and concludes that she can, though it will not be easy at first. The single sound prompted her to reconsider what she had just said.

Place of prompts. Egan's culinary metaphor: prompts should never be the main course, but they are useful condiments in the therapeutic dialogue.
sections.simple: Prompts are tiny signals, like leaning forward, nodding or saying "uh-huh", that tell clients you are with them and encourage them to continue. They work only when used on purpose, not out of habit. They are condiments, not the main course.
keyPoints: Prompts are brief verbal or nonverbal interventions showing you are with the client and encouraging more talk.
Nonverbal prompts: leaning forward, waiting, gestures, nods, eye movement (neighbour peace-overture example).
Vocal/verbal prompts: 'um', 'uh-huh', 'I see', 'okay', etc., used intentionally, not on automatic pilot.
A simple 'Um' led the perfectionistic client to reconsider her claim that she could not change.
Prompts are 'condiments', never the main course.

sections.heading: Different Forms of Probes
sections.detailed:
Used judiciously, probes help clients name, notice, explore, clarify or further define any issue at any point in helping. Their purpose is to provide clarity and move things forward. Egan describes four forms.

1. Statements. A probe can be a statement that signals the need for more clarity. A helper working with a client whose 25-year-old daughter still lives at home says it is still not clear whether the client wants to challenge her to leave the nest. The client then reveals that he wants to but fears alienating her or seeming not to care. Statement probes often take the form of the helper confessing that he or she is in the dark ("I'm not sure I understand how you intend...", "I guess I'm still confused about..."). Such probes put responsibility on clients without accusing them of holding back the truth.

2. Requests. Probes can be direct requests for more information or clarity. A counsellor asks a woman living with her husband and mother-in-law to explain what she means by "three's a crowd". She explains that she gets along with each of them separately, but the chemistry of the three together is unsettling, which is helpful new information. Requests must not sound like commands ("Come on, just tell me what you are thinking"). Tone of voice and other paralinguistic and nonverbal cues soften requests.

3. Questions. Direct questions are probably the most common probe, though Egan notes that whether they should be so common is another issue. Examples: how the client reacts when someone flies off the handle, what stops the client deciding, what a Plan B might look like. In a fuller case, a client who had built a solid anger-control programme shows hesitancy the next week. The counsellor names the hesitancy tentatively; the client fears looking like a wimp at work. The counsellor reflects that there is something about her style she does not want to lose and asks what it might be. She answers "Spunk!", and they explore keeping spunk without outbursts, that is, the practical difference between assertiveness and aggression.

4. Single words or phrases that act as questions or requests. Sometimes one word or a short phrase does the job. A client says she really hates her sister; the helper calmly repeats "Hate." The client concedes that hate is too strong and that things are simply getting worse. Another client with irrational fears declares he will "move forward"; the counsellor replies, "Move forward to...?" and the client clarifies that he means no longer indulging his fears, which he now sees as a bad habit.

Egan concludes that whatever form probes take, they are usually, directly or indirectly, questions of some sort, which is why he next discusses how to use questions.
sections.simple: Probes come in four forms: statements ("I'm not clear about..."), requests ("Tell me what you mean by..."), questions, and single words or phrases repeated back ("Hate."). All aim at clarity and moving forward, and most are really questions in disguise.
keyPoints: Probes help clients name, notice, explore, clarify or define issues; aim: clarity and forward movement.
Statements: often the helper admits being 'in the dark'; places responsibility on the client without accusing.
Requests: direct asks for information, softened by tone so they do not sound like commands.
Questions: the most common probe (anger programme / 'spunk' case: assertiveness vs aggression).
Single words/phrases: 'Hate.' and 'Move forward to...?' work as questions.
All probes are, directly or indirectly, questions of some sort.

sections.heading: Using Questions Effectively
sections.detailed:
Egan warns that helpers, especially novices and inept counsellors, ask too many questions. When unsure what to say they fire off questions that add no value, as if gathering information were the goal of the interview. Used judiciously, though, questions are an important part of helping. He gives two guidelines.

Do not ask too many questions. Clients bombarded with questions feel grilled, which harms the relationship. Many clients sense instinctively when questions are mere filler used because the helper has nothing better to say. Egan admits catching himself asking questions whose answers he did not even want to know. His case: Rolly, an inmate in a state facility for young offenders serving time for burglary and drug use. He is difficult and blames everything on his dysfunctional family. Out of frustration the counsellor asks a string of questions (when he first felt caught in the family mess, what he did to get away, what he could do differently, what friends he had). These amount to a random search for information of unclear value. Rolly, an expert at evading such questions after being grilled by professionals, simply clams up when he tires of them. Helping that becomes a question-and-answer session tends to go nowhere.

Ask open-ended questions. As a general rule, ask questions that need more than a yes/no or one-word answer. Instead of asking a newly retired person whether he has any plans, ask how he sees the future and what plans he has. Counsellors who ask closed questions end up asking more and more, because one closed question leads to another.

Exceptions. A closed question is fine when a specific piece of information is needed: a career counsellor asking how many jobs the client has had in the past two years, because it is relevant to the résumé and job-search strategy. Occasionally a sharp closed question has the right impact: a counsellor asks a client plotting revenge on his "ungrateful" son whether getting back at him is what he really wants. Such rhetorical questions are a form of challenge. If the client replies forcefully that it is, the helper learns about the intensity of his feelings and knows he faces a tricky issue.

In general, open-ended questions used in moderation help clients fill in what is missing at every stage of helping.
sections.simple: Beginners ask too many questions, which makes clients feel grilled (as with Rolly, who just clams up). Ask fewer questions and make them open-ended. Closed questions are fine for specific facts, and a sharp rhetorical question can serve as a challenge.
keyPoints: Novices tend to ask too many questions, as if information gathering were the goal.
Too many questions make clients feel grilled; Rolly's case shows a random search for information that goes nowhere.
Open-ended questions need more than a yes/no or one-word answer; closed questions breed more closed questions.
Closed questions are acceptable for needed specific facts (career counsellor: number of jobs in two years).
A sharp rhetorical question ('Is getting back at him what you really want?') can act as a challenge.

sections.heading: Guidelines for Using Probes (1): Feedback System and Engaging Clients in Dialogue
sections.detailed:
Egan offers several guidelines that apply to all probes, whatever their form. The first two concern using feedback and helping clients take part in the dialogue.

Use your ongoing feedback system as a way of probing. Whether a helper uses surveys such as Duncan's or another systematic way of getting client feedback on progress, outcomes and the quality of sessions, the feedback system is an excellent opportunity to probe. Egan illustrates with Letta, a single mother who lost a well-paid job in the economic crash. A "hip" drinker in good times, she became a problem drinker when things turned sour, had no financial cushion and spent much time railing against those blamed for the crash. Her "individually" rating was low in session one, rose sharply in session two because she thought counselling was the answer, and in session three fell below the first.

The helper uses the drop as a probe, asking what message the score carries and noting her face and posture. Letta describes soaring hopes followed by default notices, a pay cut and her boyfriend calling her "scary". The helper mixes empathy ("you soared, then the crash") with single-word and request probes ("Shot down?", "Tell me more about that"). She sees how much work lies ahead. The helper then acknowledges the misery but asks what good might be mined from it. After saying "Nothing!" and a silence, she suggests she could become more realistic, and they explore what a "realistic" lifestyle would look like. At the end-of-session survey she rates the session highly; when asked what worked, she names "realism" and links it to seeing her own self-centredness and society's habit of living beyond its means. Realism defined as concrete possibilities moved her back from the brink of "impossible", and she regained a more realistic enthusiasm.

Use probes to help clients engage as fully as possible in the therapeutic dialogue. Many clients lack the communication skills needed for the problem-managing and opportunity-developing dialogue. Egan calls probes the principal tools for helping all clients engage in the give-and-take of helping. Example: at a church parish centre a parishioner struggles to describe her dealings with her insurance company after a car accident; she feels ignored. The counsellor responds empathically and suggests reviewing what she has done so far, then asks to see the forms. They are standard claims forms. Since this is her first dealing with an insurer and her communication skills are poor, the counsellor realises her phone calls are probably part of the problem. Through empathy and probes he helps her see her experience may be normal, and she gets help from a fellow parishioner experienced with such forms.
sections.simple: Feedback ratings are a natural opening for probes: a falling score invites "What's the message?" (Letta's case). Probes are also the main tool for helping clients with weak communication skills take part in the helping dialogue (the insurance-claim parishioner).
keyPoints: Guidelines apply to all forms of probes.
Systematic feedback (e.g. Duncan's surveys) is an excellent opportunity for probing.
Letta: a falling 'individually' score opened a dialogue that turned misery into concrete 'realism'.
End-of-session feedback ('What made this session work?') is also probed.
Probes are the principal tools for helping clients with poor communication skills engage in the dialogue (insurance forms case).

sections.heading: Guidelines for Using Probes (2): Concreteness, Clarity and Clients' Points of View
sections.detailed:
Use probes to help clients achieve concreteness and clarity. Probes help clients turn the abstract and vague into something concrete and clear that both parties can work with. Egan gives three examples.

A man says his partner "treats me badly". The helper asks what she actually does. He reveals that she talks about him behind his back and cancels dates when something better comes up. Asked how he reacts, he admits they have not talked about it at all. Through empathy and probes the helper learns he tolerates a lot for fear of losing her and helps him with the psychological "economics" of a one-sided relationship.

A man dissatisfied with his poor social life says he does "funny things" that make him feel good. Asked "What kinds of things?", he describes daydreams of being a tragic hero who saves people who ignore him and then rejects them when they come running. The helper's tentative empathic summary leads him to see the contradiction: he wants to be loved but does little to build a real social life; it is all in his head. Exploring his fantasy life could be a first step to finding what he wants from relationships.

A woman who became the breadwinner after her 42-year-old husband's stroke says coming home is difficult and trails off. The helper responds empathically and asks what it is like. She describes pity for him turning into self-pity mixed with unfocused anger and rage. The probe brings out the intensity of her feelings and her desperation.

In each case the story becomes more specific. But Egan cautions that the goal is not ever more detail; it is the kind of detail that makes the problem or unused opportunity clear enough to see what can be done.

Use probes to explore and clarify clients' points of view, intentions, proposals and decisions. Clients often announce views or decisions without clarifying them, their reasons or their implications. Egan's extended case: a man badly injured in a drink-driving accident (only he was hurt), whose accident opened a Pandora's box of problems such as poor self-responsibility. Early on he argues that DUI laws are too tough because they "bully" people. The counsellor probes by asking him to imagine all such laws dropped and to add back the ones that make sense, an attempt to get him to spell out the implications of his view and begin facing himself.

Later he plans to hire an expensive lawyer to "get off". The counsellor asks for the best and then the worst outcome in court; the client has not considered the worst. The counsellor, putting himself in the client's shoes, suggests finding out how such cases usually go before spending heavily. Probes here explore the implications of a decision. The state's laws prove very tough: licence suspension for six months, a heavy fine and a month in jail. Visiting him in jail, the counsellor meets a sober, cooperative client who admits he was not ready to listen and wants to apologise to his family but does not know how. The counsellor's probe, finding out what he wants to accomplish through an apology, gives substance and order to the proposal and points it towards the future rather than the past.
sections.simple: Probes turn vague complaints into concrete, workable pictures ("Tell me what she actually does"), but the aim is useful detail, not endless detail. Probes also help clients spell out the reasons and consequences of their views and decisions, as with the drink-driving client.
keyPoints: Probes turn the abstract and vague into the concrete and clear.
Examples: partner who 'treats me badly'; daydreaming 'tragic hero'; wife of a stroke patient.
Goal is not more and more detail but detail that shows what can be done.
Probes clarify clients' points of view, intentions, proposals and decisions and their implications.
DUI case: probes on the laws, best/worst court outcomes and the purpose of an apology move him toward responsibility and the future.

sections.heading: Guidelines for Using Probes (3): Missing Pieces and a Balanced View
sections.detailed:
Use probes to help clients fill in missing pieces of the picture. Probes move the dialogue forward by helping clients identify missing parts of the problem-management puzzle: thoughts, experiences, behaviours and feelings that would give both parties a better fix on the problem situation or unused opportunity, uncover possibilities for a better future, or lead to a plan of action.

Mother-in-law case. A client at odds with his wife over his mother-in-law's visit is asked what exactly she does that angers him. He explains that she replaces the household schedule with her own and offers a constant stream of child-rearing advice; his wife sees an "inconvenience", he sees total disruption. Once her behaviour is spelled out, remedies are easier to find. But one piece is still missing: his own behaviour. Asked how he reacts, he admits he goes silent or leaves to fume, then takes it out on his wife. It becomes clear he does little to change things, and he is a little taken aback at being asked.

Divorced woman case. A woman describes her ex-husband's Sunday visits with the children ending in verbal potshots that give her headaches. The helper has a clear picture of what he does but asks what she does. She says "nothing", but further probing reveals she had raised child-support payments and criticised him for not getting a better job. She has been describing herself as total victim and him as total aggressor, which is not the full story. Her behaviour contributes to the drama; she cannot change his behaviour directly but can experiment with changing her own.

Use probes to help clients get a balanced view of problem situations and opportunities. Eager to make a point, clients often describe only one side of a picture. Probes help them fill it out. Example: a manager saddled with a bright, ambitious, aggressive young woman who plays office politics for her own ends has been agonising over his plight. The counsellor asks whether there is any upside or hidden opportunity, and, when the manager calls it a disaster, wonders aloud whether there are lessons for such a bright person. The manager reflects that he has always ignored politics, that politics exist wherever people are, and that he wants a way of dealing with it that keeps his integrity; the days of avoidance are over.

Egan draws the lesson that problem situations have a flip side: they are opportunities for rethinking and learning, and so incentives for constructive change. Here it is a chance to understand male-female dynamics at work and to explore "positive" political skills.
sections.simple: Probes help clients notice what is missing from their story, very often their own part in the problem (the mother-in-law and ex-husband cases). They also help clients see the other side of a situation, since every problem has a flip side of opportunity (the manager and office politics).
keyPoints: Probes help identify missing thoughts, experiences, behaviours and feelings in the problem-management puzzle.
Mother-in-law case: first her behaviour, then the client's own reaction (silence, fuming, blaming his wife).
Divorced woman: 'I do nothing' hides her own provocative behaviour; she can change her own part.
Probes help clients see a balanced picture rather than one side.
Manager with a political young colleague: problems have a flip side as opportunities for learning and constructive change.

sections.heading: Guidelines for Using Probes (4): Moving Through the Helping Process and Self-Challenge
sections.detailed:
Use probes to help clients move into more beneficial stages of the helping process. Probes can open dialogue about any part of helping: telling the story more fully, surfacing blind spots, setting goals, formulating strategies, discussing obstacles and reviewing actions. Many clients do not easily move to the stage that would help them most, and probes help them do so.

Sean and Fiona. A middle-aged couple who have been complaining about each other speak vaguely of "reinventing" their marriage, a term from a marriage encounter group, and hint at doing more things together. The counsellor asks what they like doing together and what the possibilities are. Fiona recalls that both like caring for others and once talked of joining the Peace Corps; Sean says those days are past. The counsellor asks "Are they?", accepts that the Peace Corps may not be an option, and has each write down three ways of helping others independently. Probes move them from tortuous problem exploration to opportunity development through brainstorming.

The affair. A woman who talks endlessly about her husband's affair (he knows she knows) says she will do nothing because it could hurt her son. The counsellor points out that doing nothing is not the only option and asks her to list what people in such situations typically do, drawing on people she knows, novels and films, without committing to any. She recalls an acquaintance who openly raised the affair at the family dinner table. The counsellor asks for more. This primes the pump; the focus on action brings energy to the session.

Jill and Justin. Justin, who lost a leg in a car accident, is letting his impairment stop him from picking up his life, and the session has bogged down. Jill proposes role reversal: she will play Justin and he will play the counsellor, asking questions that might make a difference. After a long pause Justin asks why "Justin" is taking the coward's way out and is on the verge of giving up, and his eyes fill with tears. By having Justin formulate the probes, Jill asks him to take responsibility for his part of the session. His "probes" are really challenges, almost accusations, stronger than anything Jill would have tried at that stage. Painful as it is, it is a breakthrough.

Use probes to invite clients to challenge themselves. Chapter 4 showed that empathic responses can act as a mild form of social influence or challenge, and that good responses often work as probes, indirect requests for information or ways of steering clients to a more productive stage. Probes can go further, close to outright invitations to self-challenge. Many probes are not simply requests for information; they place a demand on the client to respond, reflect, review or re-evaluate. Probes thus serve as a bridge between communicating understanding and helping clients challenge themselves.

Example: a client who committed to standing up to his possessive mother now seems to be weakening. The helper notes that he earlier spoke of "having it out with her" but now talks of "being reasonable with her" and asks how the two differ. After a pause the client admits to cold feet; she is a strong woman. The helper then helps him revisit his decision and, if he still wants it, strengthen his resolve. Egan concludes that probes used as mild challenges are perfectly legitimate, provided the helper knows what he or she is doing.
sections.simple: Probes can move stuck clients forward, from complaining to brainstorming options or taking responsibility (Sean and Fiona, the affair, Jill and Justin). Many probes also place a gentle demand on clients to rethink, making probes a bridge between understanding clients and helping them challenge themselves.
keyPoints: Probes help clients move into the stage of helping most useful for them (story, blind spots, goals, strategies, obstacles, review).
Sean and Fiona: brainstorming ways of helping others shifts them from problem exploration to opportunity development.
Affair case: listing standard options 'primes the pump' and brings energy through a focus on action.
Jill and Justin role reversal: Justin's own 'probes' become self-challenges and a breakthrough.
Probes place demands to respond, reflect, review or re-evaluate: a bridge from understanding to self-challenge.
Probes as mild challenges are legitimate if the helper knows what he or she is doing.

sections.heading: The Relationship Between Sharing Empathic Responses and Using Probes
sections.detailed:
Teaching skills one at a time takes each out of context. In real sessions skills must be blended naturally: skilled helpers continually tune in, listen actively and mix probes with empathy to help clients clarify concerns, deal with blind spots, set goals, make plans and get things done. There is no formula for the right mix; it depends on the client, the client's needs, the problem situation, possible opportunities and the stage of helping.

The basic guideline. After a probe to which the client responds, respond with empathy to what the client says and check your understanding. Be hesitant to follow one probe with another. Egan gives two reasons: (1) an effective probe yields information that needs to be listened to and understood; (2) an accurate empathic response itself places a demand on the client to explore further; it puts the ball back in the client's court.

Chinese American client: Counsellor A versus Counsellor B. A young Chinese American woman, whose father died in China and whose mother is dying in the United States, talks about the subservience common among Chinese women, her fear of slipping into passivity in her American life, and her sister who gives everything to her husband. The counsellor asks to what extent this self-effacing role is rooted in her culture. She says self-effacement is in her "cultural genes", that the North American style appeals to her, but that on a trip to China to meet her half-sisters she instantly felt totally Chinese again. Counsellor A follows with another probe ("What did you learn there?") and gets only an annoyed repetition: "That I am Chinese!" Counsellor B instead responds empathically: she learned how deep her cultural roots go. The client moves forward, asking what these roots mean for her life here and saying she wants to be Chinese and American at once but has not worked out how. Empathy works far better than a second probe.

Repositioning case. A single middle-aged woman whose company reinvented itself after an economic downturn keeps her job but with lower pay, longer hours and work she dislikes; she lacks computer and Internet skills for better jobs and feels stuck, stressed and depressed. The helper alternates empathy and probes: reflecting her doubts about feeling "grateful", asking what she could change in the short term (she decides to stop joining the complaining chorus), reflecting that, then asking what she might start doing. She recognises unused strengths (communication, common sense, working well with people) and the helper reflects that she might reposition herself at work. The word "repositioning" energises her. The combination moves her from misery to naming possibilities for a better future.

Neither machine nor interrogator. Helpers should become neither an empathic response "machine" grinding out one reflection after another nor an "interrogator" peppering clients with needless probes. All responses, including probes and challenges, are empathic if based on solid understanding of the client's core messages and points of view. Responses that build on and add to the client's remarks are implicitly empathic, which reduces the need for a constant stream of explicit empathic responses.

Box 5.1: Guidelines in using probes. Keep in mind the goals of probing; use probes to help clients: engage as fully as possible in the dialogue; help nonassertive or reluctant clients tell their stories and engage in problem-managing behaviour; identify experiences, behaviours and feelings that give focus to their stories; open up new areas for discussion; explore and clarify stories, feelings, points of view, decisions and proposals; be as concrete and specific as possible; stay focused on relevant and important issues; move on to a further stage of helping. Further, use probes as nudges or mild challenges for clients to examine how they think and act in and outside sessions; probe in the spirit of empathy; use a mix of statements, open-ended questions, prompts and requests, not questions alone; follow a successful probe with an empathic response rather than another probe; and use whatever judicious mixture of empathy and probing is needed to clarify problems, identify blind spots, develop new scenarios, search for strategies, formulate plans and review outcomes.
sections.simple: In real sessions empathy and probing are mixed, with no fixed formula. The key rule: after a probe works, respond with empathy instead of firing another probe (Counsellor B succeeded where Counsellor A failed). Avoid being either an empathy machine or an interrogator. Box 5.1 sums up the guidelines.
keyPoints: Skills must be blended naturally; the right mix depends on client, needs, situation, opportunities and stage.
Guideline: follow a probe the client answers with an empathic response; be hesitant to follow a probe with a probe.
Reasons: probes yield information that needs understanding; accurate empathy puts the ball back in the client's court.
Chinese American client: Counsellor A's second probe gets an annoyed repetition; Counsellor B's empathy moves her forward.
Don't be an empathic response 'machine' or an 'interrogator'; responses built on understanding are implicitly empathic.
Box 5.1 lists the goals of probing and rules: mix forms, probe in the spirit of empathy, follow probes with empathy.

sections.heading: The Art of Summarizing: Providing Focus and Direction
sections.detailed:
Egan introduces the last basic communication skill. The skills of visibly tuning in, listening, responding with empathy and probing must be orchestrated so that clients focus on issues that make a difference. The ability to summarise, and to help clients summarise, the main points of an interchange or session can provide both focus and challenge.

Summaries thus serve two purposes at once. They pull scattered material together so the client can see what matters (focus and direction), and, because a summary places the material in front of the client in a new way, they often nudge the client to move on or face something (challenge). Two forms are discussed: helper-provided summaries, used at particular moments, and summaries the client is asked to provide.

Link with nudging. Like probes, summaries are among the gentle nudges described at the start of the chapter: they put the ball in the client's court without forcing any option.
sections.simple: Summarising pulls together the main points of a session so clients can focus on what matters. It provides both focus and a mild challenge, and can be done by the helper or by the client.
keyPoints: Tuning in, listening, empathy and probing must be orchestrated to focus clients on issues that make a difference.
Summarising the main points of an interchange or session provides focus and challenge.
Helpers can summarise, or help clients summarise.
Summaries act as nudges that put responsibility back on the client.

sections.heading: When to Use Summaries
sections.detailed:
Brammer (1973) listed goals that summarising can serve: "warming up" the client, focusing scattered thoughts and feelings, closing discussion of a particular theme, and prompting the client to explore a theme more thoroughly. Egan names three times when summaries are especially useful.

1. At the beginning of a new session. Especially when clients seem unsure how to start, an opening summary stops them simply repeating what was said before and pressures them to move on. Liz, a social worker, opens a session with an over-talkative man by summarising the main points of the previous session. This (a) shows she listened carefully and reflected afterwards, (b) gives him a jumping-off point and a chance to add to or modify what was said, and (c) places responsibility for moving forward on him. The implied message is "Now where do you want to go with this?" Summaries put the ball in the client's court and invite initiative. Getting client feedback at the beginning and end of each session also makes the flow between sessions smoother.

2. During a session that is going nowhere. A main reason sessions stall is that helpers let clients go over the same ground instead of going deeper, focusing on possibilities and goals, or discussing strategies. Marcia, a coach, consultant and counsellor working with staff at a homeless shelter, meets a staff member showing signs of burnout who keeps recounting stressful incidents, such as being hit by someone she was helping and heated arguments with coworkers. Marcia summarises: the work is stressful by nature, such incidents are part of the furniture in shelters and will not stop, they are punishing, and so the real questions are how to cope, how to get ongoing satisfaction, and what changes might reduce incidents. The purpose is to move the client beyond "poor me" toward coping. Egan adds that the challenge in such settings is building a supportive work environment, a sense of organisational and personal purpose, mission-fitting teamwork and a culture of coping strategies.

3. When the client needs a new perspective. Pulling scattered elements together often lets the client see the bigger picture. A man reluctant to attend counselling with his wife agrees to a couple of sessions "to please her" and talks disjointedly about home. The counsellor gathers the points: he encourages her career and her time with friends, spends time with the kids, handles the finances, accepts or rejects social invitations because his schedule is tighter, and now wants her to move to Boston for his better job. The client realises it sounds as if he is running her life. The summary gives a mild jolt; he must face the theme that he makes many decisions, some big, for her. (New perspectives are the focus of Chapter 6.)

A second example: a 52-year-old single man who is "down in the dumps" hears a summary of his persistent slump, health worries that seem a symptom rather than cause, loss of old friends after a job change leaving a bleak social life, a painful struggle to stay young, and "over investing" in work so that life feels empty when a project ends. He finds it painful but accurate, admits to "screwed-up values", and agrees to look at what a better future might be like. The client draws his own conclusion.

Cautions. Do not overwhelm clients with the content of a summary, and never use summaries to "build a case" against a client; helping is not a judicial procedure. Egan suggests the last summary might have worked better had it also included the client's strengths, giving a more positive context.
sections.simple: Brammer listed goals of summaries such as warming up the client and focusing scattered thoughts. Summaries help most at the start of a session (Liz), when a session is going nowhere (Marcia), and when a client needs a new perspective (the husband "running her life"). Don't overwhelm the client or build a case against them; include strengths.
keyPoints: Brammer (1973): summaries warm up the client, focus scattered thoughts and feelings, close a theme, prompt deeper exploration.
At the start of a session (Liz): shows listening, gives a jumping-off point, puts responsibility on the client.
When a session goes nowhere (Marcia at the shelter): moves the client beyond 'poor me' to coping.
When a new perspective is needed: husband sees he is 'running her life'; 52-year-old man sees his values.
Do not overwhelm clients or 'build a case'; helping is not a judicial procedure; include strengths.

sections.heading: Getting the Client to Provide the Summary
sections.detailed:
Summaries are useful when clients do not seem to know where to go next, either within the session or in a real-world action programme. Probes could be used to help them move on, but summaries have a way of keeping the ball in the client's court.

The helper need not always supply the summary. Often it is better to ask the client to pull the major points together. This helps the client own the helping process, gather the salient points and move on. Because the exercise is not a test, the counsellor should give the client whatever help is needed to stitch the summary together.

Example: a client who lost her job and her boyfriend because of alcohol-induced outbursts of anger has been talking about "not being able to stick to the program". The counsellor asks her to summarise what she has been doing and the obstacles she has met. With help, she stumbles through it and concludes that she clearly has not been sticking to the programme: on paper the plan looked easy, but she does not "live on paper". She then uses the counsellor to step back and review her goals, plans, obstacles and execution.
sections.simple: Instead of summarising for the client, the helper can ask the client to summarise. This helps the client own the process and move on. It is not a test, so the helper should help as needed.
keyPoints: Useful when clients do not know where to go next in the session or in an action programme.
Summaries keep the ball in the client's court.
Asking the client to summarise helps them own the process, gather salient points and move on.
It is not a test; the helper helps the client stitch the summary together.
Alcohol/anger client: 'I don't live on paper' leads to reviewing goals, plans, obstacles and execution.

sections.heading: Mara and Carlos Revisited
sections.detailed:
Egan returns to his running case. Carlos uses probes throughout to help Mara gain depth and clarity on key issues. Suspecting that her visit to Iran holds guidelines for her own future, he suggests reviewing what she learned there.

Probing the Iran experience. Mara expected young Iranians to be depressed given a tough economy and less freedom, but Carlos reflects that she found they had their own kind of freedom. She describes them as upbeat, critical of the government and of overly controlling religious leaders but not of the religion itself, wanting a better economy yet talking about ideas instead of merely complaining, and loving their culture without feeling constrained by it; in some ways freer than she feels. When Carlos remarks that even their complaining sounds positive, she says she does not want to idealise it, and Carlos reflects that it nonetheless spoke to her strongly. She agrees: it showed her what is lacking in her own life. Carlos names "the contrast" and her "cultural ghetto" feeling. She envied their lively families and communities of friends; her own home has never been lively, and it is worse after the disastrous conversation with her father. Carlos reflects that finding or creating her own version of this is central to her desired future. Carlos combines empathy and probes and also helps her explore her relationship with her mother.

Client-provided summary. To help her "reset the system" after the conversation with her father, Carlos suggests she summarise what has happened and what she has learned. Since it is near the end of the session, she chooses to think it over and open the next session with her summary, which Carlos invites with "Where do we stand today?"

Her summary: she has been naive in carving out a future; she is now more realistic and determined, yet more fearful. Carlos reflects that she is wiser but the view is daunting. Her dilemma: she wants a full career and social life, but her parents see this as betrayal, they are ageing and her father's health is uncertain; it feels like a culture clash between the American who wants to move on and the dutiful Iranian daughter, though she knows that is too simplistic. Carlos suggests it may still be a useful simple framework, and she calls it a tool or map. Probed on her social life, she says "the equation is wrong": home life plus work life equals her social life; she lacks friends her age, a friendship community and intimate friends, her aunt is busy and her cousins too consumerist. Carlos reflects that the work-social balance needs immediate attention and asks for positives: she feels secure at home and work, though it is a lifeless security, and her strongest asset is her desire for a more engaging community. Her friend Jim is getting divorced, but he is "not the one". They then review her career aspirations and what it is like to be a "cultural hybrid".

Her main challenge: she feels she cannot follow her heart in social or work life without in some sense abandoning her parents, which she does not want to do. Carlos frames the search as finding a way to pursue career and social life without abandoning them, and probes where "not always pleasing them" fits. Egan concludes that the issues are now fairly clear: Mara knows what she wants but cannot yet see how to get it, and figuring that out is the challenge.
sections.simple: Carlos uses empathy and probes to help Mara see what her trip to Iran revealed about what is missing in her own life: community and lively relationships. He then has Mara summarise her situation herself, which clarifies her core dilemma: building her own life without abandoning her parents.
keyPoints: Carlos probes Mara's Iran trip for hints about her own future.
Contrast with upbeat, community-rich young Iranians highlights her 'cultural ghetto' feeling.
Carlos asks Mara to summarise; she opens the next session with her own summary.
Her dilemma: American who wants to move on vs dutiful Iranian daughter; 'the equation is wrong' in her social life.
Main challenge: following her heart without abandoning her parents; she knows what she wants but not how to get it.

sections.heading: The Shadow Side of Communication Skills: Communication Skills as Necessary but Not Sufficient
sections.detailed:
Egan notes that the chapters so far have covered basic communication skills; Chapter 6 will move to advanced skills and processes that help clients move beyond blind spots to new perspectives, life-enhancing outcomes and action. Before that, he revisits the shadow side of communication skills under the heading "essential, but not everything".

Overidentifying helping with communication skills. Some training programmes and helpers equate the helping process with the communication skills that serve it. These skills are critical tools, but being good at communication skills is not the same as being good at helping. An overemphasis on them can turn helping into a lot of talk with little action and few outcomes that make a real difference to clients' lives.

Skills must serve process and outcomes. Communication skills are essential, but they must serve both the process and the outcomes of helping. They help build a good relationship, and a good relationship is the basis for the social-emotional re-education outlined earlier in the book. Yet a helper can be good at communication, relationship building and even social-emotional re-education and still shortchange clients, because clients need more than that.

Two kinds of overestimation. Some helpers treat a skill such as empathic responding as a "magic bullet"; others overestimate the value of information gathering. Egan stresses that this is not a sweeping indictment of the profession but a caution for beginners.
sections.simple: Communication skills are essential tools, but being good at them is not the same as being good at helping. Overemphasising them can produce lots of talk and little action. Empathy is no "magic bullet" and information gathering is not the goal.
keyPoints: Chapter 6 will cover advanced skills; first Egan revisits the shadow side of communication skills.
Some programmes overidentify helping with communication skills; skill at communicating is not skill at helping.
Overemphasis can create much talk, little action and few meaningful outcomes.
Skills build the relationship, the basis for social-emotional re-education, but clients need more than that.
Some see empathy as a 'magic bullet'; others overvalue information gathering; a caution for beginners.

sections.heading: The Helping Relationship Versus Helping Technologies
sections.detailed:
The opposite error is to underestimate the need for solid communication skills. Some practitioners quietly assume that the "technology" of their approach, such as treatment manuals, is enough. They listen and respond through their theories and constructs rather than through their humanity, becoming technologists instead of helpers. Egan compares them to some medical doctors who grow ever more proficient with medical technology and ever less in touch with their patients' humanity.

Egan's hospital experience. Some years earlier Egan spent ten days in hospital (an eternity in the age of managed care). The staff handled his medical needs magnificently, but the psychological needs arising from anxiety about his illness were not addressed at all. Because his anxieties often showed up as physical symptoms, those symptoms were then treated medically. Frustrated, he asked the young doctor debriefing him about the staffing conference whether, after reviewing a patient's medical status, the team ever turned to what the patient was going through and how to help him through it. The resident replied that they did not have time. Egan emphasises that these were dedicated, generous people with his interests at heart, yet they ignored many of his needs. He sees involving healthcare psychologists in staffing sessions as a step in the right direction, and reports that on more recent visits to the same centre his experience was strikingly different: the medical profession's newer focus on relationship skills had become part of the centre's culture.

Taken with the previous section, the message is balance: communication skills are necessary but not sufficient, and technique without relationship is equally inadequate.
sections.simple: The opposite mistake is relying on techniques and manuals and forgetting the human relationship, so that helpers become technologists. Egan's hospital stay, where his medical needs were met but his anxiety was ignored, shows the cost.
keyPoints: Some practitioners underestimate communication skills and assume their approach's 'technology' (e.g. manuals) suffices.
They respond through theories and constructs, not their humanity: technologists instead of helpers.
Like doctors expert in technology but out of touch with patients' humanity.
Egan's 10-day hospital stay: medical needs met, psychological needs ignored; 'we don't have time'.
Healthcare psychologists in staffing sessions help; later visits showed relationship skills had entered the culture.

sections.heading: Developing Proficiency in Communication Skills
sections.detailed:
Understanding communication skills and how they fit into helping is one thing; becoming proficient in them is another. Some trainees assume these "soft" skills are easy and fail to put in the hard work and practice needed to become fluent. Doing manual exercises and practising in training groups helps but is not enough to make the skills second nature. Tuning in, listening, processing, sharing highlights and probing that are brought out only for helping sessions are likely to ring hollow. The skills must become part of the helper's everyday communication style and grow from a commitment to empathic relationships.

Practise in real life. After initial training Egan tells students to go out into their real lives and get good at these skills, since he cannot do it for them. Practising them in daily life may be hard at first not because they are difficult but because they are rare in ordinary conversation. Take empathic responding: if you pressed an unobtrusive counter each time you heard someone give an empathic response, you might go days without pressing it. Yet you can make empathy part of your own life, and others will notice, though they will not call it empathy; they will say things like "She really listens to me" or "He takes me seriously."

Probes in everyday life. By contrast, probes, usually questions, are everywhere, because people are more comfortable asking questions than offering understanding. But many everyday probes are aimless, and worse, many are disguised criticisms ("Why on earth did you do that?"). Learning to integrate purposeful probes with empathy takes practice in daily life. Egan's slogan: life is your lab, and every conversation is an opportunity.

Relevance beyond counselling. These skills belong in all human transactions, including business. When businesses list competencies they want in applicants, especially managers, communication and relationship-building skills are almost always at or near the top. Egan once trained an accounting firm; the training director valued the skills, but many account managers resisted. One notable resister later called to say he "owed" Egan a call. Meeting a prospective client dissatisfied with its audit firm, and thinking they had no chance of the account, he decided to amuse himself by trying the skills. The client gave his firm the account, saying it was not because they were the lowest bidder (they were not) but because they were the only ones who really understood the client's needs. Egan jokes that he forgot to ask for a share of the fee.
sections.simple: Knowing the skills is not the same as being good at them. They must be practised in everyday life until they become your natural style, since empathy is rare and aimless or critical questions are common. "Life is your lab." These skills even win business, as the accounting firm story shows.
keyPoints: Understanding skills is different from proficiency; 'soft' skills need hard work and practice.
Manuals and training groups are not enough; skills used only in sessions sound hollow.
Skills must become part of everyday style, rooted in commitment to empathic relationships.
Empathy is rare in daily talk (the counter exercise); probes are common but often aimless or disguised criticism.
'Life is your lab. Every conversation is an opportunity.'
Business values these skills: the resistant accountant won an account because the client felt understood.

terms.definition: Following Thaler and Sunstein, any feature of the choice architecture that changes behaviour in a predictable way without forbidding any options.
Thaler and Sunstein's label for influence that guides people (paternalism, without coercion) while preserving their freedom of choice (libertarian, but not 'do whatever you want').
Someone responsible for organising the context in which people make decisions; helpers are inevitably choice architects for their clients.
The context in which decisions are made; Egan treats treatment models, including the Skilled Helper framework and its skills, as forms of choice architecture.
Because helpers cannot respond empathically to everything, choosing what to respond to is itself a form of influence, one way empathy acts as a nudge.
Egan's description of nudges: they have power but do not overwhelm clients, foster collaboration and keep clients at the centre of decisions.
Verbal and sometimes nonverbal tactics that help clients talk more freely and concretely about any issue at any stage of helping; they provide clarity and move things forward.
Brief verbal or nonverbal interventions that let clients know the helper is with them and encourage them to talk further.
Bodily movements, gestures, nods, eye movements, leaning forward and waiting that work as nudges to keep a client talking.
Sounds and words such as 'um', 'uh-huh', 'I see' or 'okay', effective only when used intentionally rather than on automatic pilot.
A probe phrased as a statement of the need for more clarity, often the helper confessing confusion; it places responsibility on the client without accusing.
A direct request for more information or clarity ('Tell me what you mean...'), softened by tone so it does not sound like a command.
A direct question; perhaps the most common type of probe, though Egan doubts it should be so common.
A single word or short phrase (e.g. repeating 'Hate.' or 'Move forward to...?') that functions as a question or request.
A question that requires more than a yes/no or similar one-word answer; recommended as the general rule.
A question answerable with yes/no or one word; tends to lead to more closed questions but is appropriate when specific information is needed.
A sharp closed question used as a form of challenge, e.g. 'Is getting back at him what you really want?'
What clients feel when they are asked too many questions; it harms the relationship and leads clients like Rolly to clam up.
Systematic client feedback (e.g. Duncan's surveys) on progress, outcomes and session quality, which Egan says is an excellent opportunity for probing.
Turning what is abstract and vague into something concrete and clear that helper and client can work with; a key aim of probing.
Thoughts, experiences, behaviours and feelings absent from a client's account (often the client's own behaviour) that probes help fill in.
Seeing both sides of a problem situation or opportunity rather than the one side clients tend to describe.
The idea that problem situations are also opportunities for rethinking and learning, and so incentives for constructive change.
Probes that place a demand on clients to respond, reflect, review or re-evaluate, serving as a bridge between understanding and challenge.
A helper who mechanically grinds out one empathic response after another; one of two extremes to avoid.
A helper who peppers clients with needless probes; the other extreme to avoid.
Responses, including probes and challenges, that build on and add to a client's remarks and rest on solid understanding of core messages.
Pulling together the main points of an interchange or session, by the helper or the client, to provide focus, direction and challenge.
A summary the client is asked to give, which helps the client own the process; the helper assists because it is not a test.
Carlos's phrase for Mara's sense of what was missing in her own life when contrasted with the lively communities she saw in Iran.
Mara's description of her experience of being both American and Iranian.
The process outlined earlier in the book for which a good helping relationship, built on communication skills, is the basis.
Egan's term for the mistaken belief that a single skill, such as empathic responding, can by itself make helping effective.
Practitioners who rely on the 'technology' of their approach (e.g. treatment manuals) and respond through theory rather than their humanity.
Egan's slogan for practising communication skills in everyday conversations until they become second nature.

examples.title: A nudge in a college counselling room
examples.text: A first-year student says she is thinking of dropping out of her engineering course. The counsellor neither forbids it nor pushes it, but asks her to list what she would be moving toward if she left. All options stay open, yet the question predictably steers her to think about goals rather than escape.

examples.title: Statement vs grilling with an anxious parent
examples.text: Instead of firing questions at a mother worried about her son's board exams ('How many hours does he study? Does he use his phone? Does he sleep late?'), the counsellor says, 'I'm still not clear what worries you most about this.' She replies that her real fear is family comparison with a cousin, something no question in the list would have found.

examples.title: Following a probe with empathy
examples.text: Counsellor: 'What happens at home when your marks come?' Client: 'Appa doesn't shout. He just stops talking to me for days.' A second probe ('How many days?') would stall things. An empathic reply ('The silence hurts more than shouting would') invites the client to say more.

examples.title: Summary at the start of a session
examples.text: A counsellor opens: 'Last week you spoke about the hostel noise, missing your family in Mangaluru and feeling behind in two subjects. Where would you like to go with this today?' The client, who usually repeats the same complaints, picks the subjects and starts planning.
