practice.q: What is meant by a 'nudge' in helping?
practice.answer: Following Thaler and Sunstein (2008), Egan defines a nudge as any aspect of the choice architecture that alters behaviour in a predictable way without forbidding any options. Helpers inevitably influence clients, and probes, summaries and even empathic responses act as nudges with 'gentle power' that keeps clients at the centre of decision making.

A term from Thaler and Sunstein's Nudge, used by Egan for the influence helpers exercise. It is paternalistic because the helper influences the client, though without physical or psychological coercion, and libertarian because the client's freedom of choice is preserved, though this does not mean 'do whatever you want'.

practice.q: What are prompts? Give two examples.
practice.answer: Prompts are brief verbal or nonverbal interventions that let clients know the helper is with them and encourage further talk. Examples: leaning forward attentively and waiting after a client says "I just can't do it!", or a brief, intentional "Um" that led a perfectionistic client to reconsider her claim that she could not change. They are condiments, not the main course.

Open-ended questions require more than a yes/no or one-word answer ("How do you see the future?") and are Egan's general rule. Closed questions invite one-word answers and tend to breed more closed questions, though they are appropriate when specific information is needed (number of jobs in two years) or as a sharp rhetorical challenge.

practice.q: What does Egan mean by 'Life is your lab'?
practice.answer: Communication skills become second nature only through practice in everyday life, not just in manuals or training groups. Since empathy is rare and aimless or critical probes are common in daily talk, every conversation is a chance to practise integrating purposeful probes with empathy.

practice.q: Explain the different forms of probes with examples.
practice.answer:
Egan describes probes as verbal and sometimes nonverbal tactics that help clients name, notice, explore, clarify or further define issues at any stage of helping. Their aim is clarity and forward movement. They take four forms.

Statements. A statement signals the need for more clarity, often as the helper admitting confusion: "It's still not clear to me whether you want to challenge her to leave the nest." Such probes put responsibility on the client without accusing him or her of withholding.

Requests. Direct requests for information, such as "Tell me what you mean when you say three's a crowd at home," which brought out that the client's difficulty lay in the three-way chemistry with husband and mother-in-law. Requests must not sound like commands; tone and nonverbal cues soften them.

Questions. Probably the most common probe. In one case a client backtracking on an anger-control programme was asked what she did not want to lose; she said "Spunk!", which opened a discussion of assertiveness versus aggression.

Single words or phrases. Repeating "Hate." led a client to admit the word was too strong; "Move forward to...?" helped a fearful client specify his goal.

Egan concludes that all these are, directly or indirectly, questions, so the rules for using questions apply to every form.

practice.q: Discuss Egan's guidelines for using questions effectively.
practice.answer:
Egan observes that novices and inept counsellors ask too many questions, often when unsure what to do, as though gathering information were the purpose of the interview. Used judiciously, though, questions are valuable. He offers two guidelines.

Do not ask too many questions. Clients who are bombarded feel grilled, and many sense when questions are filler. Egan admits asking questions whose answers he did not want. In the case of Rolly, a young offender who blames his dysfunctional family, the frustrated counsellor fires a string of questions about his family and friends. These are a random search for information; Rolly, used to being grilled by professionals, clams up. Question-and-answer helping goes nowhere.

Ask open-ended questions. Questions should need more than a yes/no answer: not "Do you have any plans?" but "How do you see the future? What plans do you have?" Closed questions generate more closed questions.

Exceptions. A closed question is right when specific information is needed, as when a career counsellor asks how many jobs a client has had in two years for a résumé. A sharp rhetorical question ("Is getting back at him what you really want?") can act as a challenge and reveal the intensity of feelings.

Thus open-ended questions in moderation help clients fill in what is missing at every stage.

practice.q: Explain the concept of nudging and its relevance to counselling.
practice.answer:
Egan begins from the premise that all helping involves influence. The challenge is to influence clients to discuss difficult issues, develop new perspectives, choose goals and act, without robbing them of their freedom.

He borrows from Thaler and Sunstein's Nudge (2008). Their term libertarian paternalism describes influence that is paternalistic but not coercive, and libertarian without meaning "anything goes". A choice architect organises the context in which people decide. Because decision making is central to therapy and helpers cannot avoid influence, helpers are choice architects; treatment models, including the Skilled Helper framework, its methods and skills, are forms of choice architecture.

A nudge alters behaviour predictably (in the social-science sense) without forbidding options. Even empathy nudges: selective responding influences what clients attend to, and empathic responses encourage broader and deeper exploration, without pinning clients down.

Nudges have "gentle power". Used skilfully they encourage collaboration, do not overwhelm and keep clients at the centre of decision making. Egan presents probing and summarising as two key nudges, which links the idea to the whole chapter and gives an ethical frame for influence in counselling.

practice.q: Explain the relationship between sharing empathic responses and using probes.
practice.answer:
Egan notes that teaching skills separately takes them out of context; in real sessions helpers continually tune in, listen and blend probes with empathy. There is no formula: the mix depends on the client, needs, situation, opportunities and stage.

Basic guideline. After a client responds to a probe, respond with empathy and check understanding; be hesitant to follow one probe with another. First, an effective probe yields information that needs to be understood. Second, accurate empathy places a demand on the client to explore further, putting the ball back in the client's court.

Illustration. A Chinese American woman describes feeling totally Chinese on a trip to China. Counsellor A asks another probe, "What did you learn there?", and gets an annoyed "That I am Chinese!" Counsellor B reflects, "You learned just how deep your cultural roots go," and she moves on to how to be Chinese and American at once. In a second case, alternating empathy and probes helps a stressed employee move from misery to "repositioning" herself using unused skills.

Helpers should be neither an empathy "machine" nor an "interrogator". Any response grounded in understanding of the client's core messages is implicitly empathic. Box 5.1 summarises these guidelines.

practice.q: When should a counsellor use summaries? Illustrate.
practice.answer:
Egan sees summarising as a skill that provides focus and challenge. Brammer (1973) listed its goals: warming up the client, focusing scattered thoughts and feelings, closing a theme and prompting deeper exploration. Egan highlights three occasions.

Beginning of a session. Summaries stop clients repeating old material and press them to move on. Liz, a social worker, summarises the previous session for a talkative client: this shows she listened and reflected, offers a jumping-off point and places responsibility on him ("Now where do you want to go with this?").

A session going nowhere. Marcia, working with a burnt-out shelter worker who keeps recounting incidents, summarises that such incidents are part of the furniture, then poses questions about coping and change, moving her beyond "poor me".

When a new perspective is needed. Pulling together a husband's scattered comments (he handles finances, decides on invitations, plans a move to Boston) leads him to see he may be running his wife's life. A 52-year-old man hears a summary of his slump and admits to "screwed-up values".

Cautions: do not overwhelm clients, never "build a case", and include strengths. Clients can also be asked to provide the summary, which helps them own the process.

practice.q: 'Communication skills are essential but not everything.' Discuss.
practice.answer:
Under the shadow side of communication skills, Egan warns against two opposite errors.

Necessary but not sufficient. Some training programmes and helpers overidentify helping with communication skills, which are only its tools. Being good at communication is not being good at helping, and overemphasis yields much talk, little action and few meaningful outcomes. Skills build the relationship that underpins social-emotional re-education, but clients need more. Some treat empathy as a "magic bullet"; others overvalue information gathering. Egan frames this as a caution for beginners, not an indictment of the profession.

Relationship versus technologies. Other practitioners underestimate communication skills and rely on the "technology" of their approach, such as manuals, responding through theory rather than humanity: technologists instead of helpers, like doctors expert in equipment but out of touch with patients. Egan's ten-day hospital stay illustrates this: excellent medical care, but his anxiety was ignored and its physical symptoms treated medically; the resident said they had "no time". Later visits showed relationship skills had become part of the centre's culture.

The lesson is balance: skills must serve the process and outcomes of helping.

practice.q: Describe the guidelines for using probes in counselling, with suitable illustrations from Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan describes probes as verbal and sometimes nonverbal tactics that help clients talk more freely and concretely about any issue at any stage of helping. If empathy is the lubricant of dialogue, probes provide the needed nudges. Probes may be statements, requests, questions or single words, and Egan offers guidelines that apply to all of them.

1. Use the ongoing feedback system to probe. Systematic feedback, such as Duncan's surveys, is an excellent opening. When Letta's "individually" score fell below her first-session level, the helper asked what message it carried. Mixing empathy with probes like "Shot down?" and "What good might come from all of this?" led her to the idea of "realism", which she later named as what made the session work.

2. Help clients engage in the dialogue. Many clients lack the communication skills for problem-managing dialogue; probes are the principal tools for drawing them in. A parishioner frustrated with her insurer was helped to review what she had done and show her forms, revealing that her experience was normal.

3. Achieve concreteness and clarity. "Tell me what she actually does" turned a vague complaint into specific behaviours and revealed the client's fear of losing his partner. "What kinds of things?" uncovered a client's tragic-hero daydreams. The aim is not endless detail but detail that shows what can be done.

4. Clarify points of view, intentions, proposals and decisions. With a drink-driving client, probes about DUI laws and the best and worst court outcomes helped him face the implications of his views and decisions; later a probe about what an apology should achieve gave his proposal substance.

5. Fill in missing pieces. Probes revealed what a man did when his mother-in-law disrupted the household (going silent, then blaming his wife) and that a divorced woman who said she did "nothing" was in fact provoking her ex-husband.

6. Get a balanced view. Asking a manager about any "upside" to his political young colleague helped him see the flip side: problems are opportunities for learning.

7. Move into more beneficial stages. Probes moved Sean and Fiona from complaints to brainstorming ways of helping others, primed the pump for a woman stuck on her husband's affair, and, through role reversal, let Justin pose his own challenging "probes".

8. Invite self-challenge. Probes place demands on clients to reflect and re-evaluate, bridging understanding and challenge, as when a client was asked how "having it out" with his mother differed from "being reasonable" with her.

Box 5.1 adds: keep the goals of probing in mind; probe in the spirit of empathy; mix statements, open-ended questions, prompts and requests rather than relying on questions; follow a successful probe with empathy, not another probe; and use whatever mix of empathy and probing helps clients clarify problems, see blind spots, develop scenarios, plan and review.

Conclusion. For Egan, probing is a disciplined skill that gives focus and direction to the whole helping process. Used judiciously and within an empathic relationship, probes act as gentle nudges that deepen exploration, move clients toward action and invite self-challenge, while the helper avoids becoming an interrogator.

practice.q: Discuss summarising as a communication skill, including when to use summaries and getting clients to summarise. Illustrate with the case of Mara and Carlos.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Egan treats summarising as the skill that orchestrates tuning in, listening, empathy and probing so that clients focus on issues that make a difference. Summaries of the main points of an interchange or session provide both focus and challenge, and act as gentle nudges that put the ball in the client's court.

Goals. Brammer (1973) listed goals of summarising: warming up the client, focusing scattered thoughts and feelings, bringing a theme to a close and prompting deeper exploration.

When to use summaries. (a) At the beginning of a session, especially when clients are unsure how to start. Liz's summary for a talkative client showed she had listened and reflected, gave him a jumping-off point to add to or modify, and placed responsibility for moving forward on him. Feedback at the start and end of sessions also smooths the flow. (b) When a session is going nowhere, often because helpers let clients cover the same ground. Marcia summarised a burnt-out shelter worker's incidents as part of the furniture and reframed the issue as how to cope and what might change, moving her beyond "poor me". (c) When the client needs a new perspective. A husband hearing his scattered comments pulled together realised he might be running his wife's life; a 52-year-old man heard his slump, lost friendships, fear of ageing and over-investment in work summarised and admitted to "screwed-up values".

Cautions. Summaries should not overwhelm clients or "build a case"; helping is not a judicial procedure. Including strengths gives a more positive context.

Getting the client to summarise. When clients do not know where to go next, the helper can ask them to pull the main points together. This helps them own the process and move on; since it is not a test, the helper should help. A client whose drinking-linked anger cost her a job and boyfriend summarised her lack of progress and concluded that she does not "live on paper", then reviewed goals, plans, obstacles and execution.

Mara and Carlos. Carlos first uses empathy and probes to help Mara review her trip to Iran, where the upbeat, community-rich lives of young people highlighted her "cultural ghetto" feeling. To help her reset after the painful conversation with her father, he asks her to summarise what she has learned; she chooses to open the next session with it. Her summary covers her naivety turned into realism and fear; the clash between the American who wants to move on and the dutiful Iranian daughter; the "wrong equation" of her social life; and her desire for community. Carlos's empathic responses and probes help her reach her central challenge: following her heart without abandoning her parents. The issues become clear even though the way forward is not.

Conclusion. Summaries, whether given by helper or client, bring focus and direction, challenge clients gently and keep responsibility with them. Used at the right moments and with care, they turn scattered talk into a clearer picture from which progress can follow.

practice.q: Critically discuss the shadow side of communication skills and how helpers can develop proficiency in them.
practice.answer:
Introduction. After the basic communication skills (tuning in, listening, empathy, probing, summarising), Egan pauses before the advanced skills of Chapter 6 to examine their shadow side. His message is that these skills are "essential, but not everything", and that mastering them requires much more than classroom learning.

Necessary but not sufficient. Some training programmes and helpers overidentify helping with communication skills, which are critical tools but not the process itself. Being good at communication is not the same as being good at helping. Overemphasis turns helping into a lot of talk with little action and few outcomes that matter in clients' lives. Skills help build a good relationship, which is the basis for social-emotional re-education, yet a helper can be good at all of these and still shortchange clients, who need more. Two specific errors are treating empathy as a "magic bullet" and overvaluing information gathering, which echoes the earlier warning about asking too many questions. Egan presents this as a caution for beginners rather than an indictment of the profession.

The helping relationship versus helping technologies. The opposite error is underestimating communication skills. Some practitioners assume the "technology" of their approach, such as treatment manuals, is enough. They respond through theory rather than through their humanity and become technologists instead of helpers, like doctors who master equipment and lose touch with patients. Egan's hospital stay shows the cost: superb medical care, but his anxiety was ignored and its physical symptoms were treated medically; asked whether staff ever considered what he was going through, the resident replied there was no time. Egan stresses these were dedicated people, recommends involving healthcare psychologists in staffing sessions, and notes that later visits showed relationship skills had become part of the centre's culture.

Developing proficiency. Understanding skills differs from being proficient. Some trainees think "soft" skills come easily and skip the hard work. Manuals and training groups help but do not make skills second nature; skills brought out only for sessions ring hollow. They must become part of everyday style, rooted in commitment to empathic relationships. Egan tells students to go and get good at the skills in their real lives. Empathy is rare in daily talk (one could go days without hearing an empathic response), yet people notice when someone "really listens". Probes, by contrast, are common but often aimless or disguised criticisms ("Why on earth did you do that?"). Integrating purposeful probes with empathy needs daily practice: "Life is your lab."

Wider value. Businesses rank communication and relationship-building skills at or near the top of desired competencies. A resistant account manager trained by Egan won a new account because the client felt only his firm understood its needs.

Conclusion. Egan's stance is balanced: communication skills must serve the process and outcomes of helping, neither replacing them nor being replaced by technique. Proficiency comes from making the skills a way of life, not a set of tricks for sessions.
